caption:
Jordan Belfort, the "Wolf of Wall Street," launched Tone, an AI voice platform built on his Straight Line sales method.
It changes tone, pace and emphasis to fit the goal of a call. Belfort says it could match top human closers within a year.
It has raised about $10 million and calls only opted-in leads, he says.

paragraphs.text: Jordan Belfort, the former stockbroker known as the Wolf of Wall Street, and investor Shervin Pishevar launched Tone, an AI voice platform, on November 16, 2026, according to a Business Wire release. The product comes from Straightline.AI, where Belfort is co-founder and Pishevar is co-founder and executive chairman.

The company says Tone changes tonality, volume, speed, pacing and emphasis as a conversation develops, based on what the conversation is meant to achieve. The release gives examples: a calmer tone with a frustrated customer, a slower pace when an AI tutor explains a hard concept, and more confidence when a sales assistant explains a product.

Tone combines goal-oriented voice agents for customer service, sales, education and hospitality, expressive voice generation for audiobooks, podcasts and advertising, and voice cloning for authorized users and businesses. It is available as a research preview in English and Spanish, with API access and a self-service platform for creators.

The system draws on Belfort's Straight Line Tonality method and on U.S. Patent No. 12,437,153, titled Persuasive conversational agents for selecting words and tonalities, which was granted to Straightline.AI in October 2025, according to the release.

A self-service product lets authors and creators turn books into AI narration, using Tone's voices or, once cloning rolls out, their own. Belfort said cloning requires creators to speak into the system and sign consent, with uploaded recordings checked against a live voiceprint, according to Superpower Daily's summary of TechCrunch's interview.

Belfort told reporters that Tone could catch top human salespeople within six months to a year, while saying it has not reached that level yet, TokenPost reported. He gave no close rates or comparison data.

He said customers include law firms, health insurers and polling and auto businesses, without naming them. He estimated revenue at roughly $700,000 to $1 million, without a time period, and said the company has raised about $10 million from friends, family and seed investors. The response delay is about 600 milliseconds, using small models that he acknowledged are less capable than frontier systems.

Belfort said the system calls only leads who opted in or existing customers. Federal Communications Commission rules apply consent requirements for artificial or prerecorded voices to AI-generated voices, TokenPost noted.

Belfort pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont. Neither co-founder is an engineer, and the performance of the technology could not be independently verified, Dealroom reported.

Most of the business figures come from Belfort himself, so the product's results remain unproven. The launch adds a well-known name to a crowded voice agent market, where the main pitch is persuasion rather than accuracy.
The next test is whether Tone publishes measurable results, such as close rates against human sales teams, once the research preview opens wider.
